summary: This standards-track memo describes how to carry real-time text conversation, as specified in ITU-T T.140, in RTP packets. It obsoletes RFC 2793 and describes a payload format for sending text on its own RTP session.

eli5.summary: Like a live chat where letters appear as typed, this says how to send them over the internet in packets, so people can talk by text in real time.

questions: how does rtp text redundancy work
what is the cps parameter in sdp
what clock rate does text/t140 use
subtitle: How to send live, character-by-character text chat over RTP, with built-in repetition to survive lost packets.

tldr.problem: Real-time text conversation (ITU-T T.140) needs characters to arrive in order, without duplicates and with any loss noticed, while the text itself is tiny compared with packet overhead.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP packet carries one block of UTF-8 T.140 text with no extra framing, sent on its own RTP session. By default RFC 2198 redundancy repeats the text from earlier packets, so a lost packet can usually be rebuilt from the next one.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4103 obsoletes RFC 2793 and clarifies it. It has since been updated by RFC 9071.

facts.label: Recommended buffering time
facts.value: 300 ms (500 ms is the T.140 maximum)

facts.label: Default redundancy
facts.value: Original text plus two redundant generations

facts.label: Recommended wait for a missing packet

today: RFC 4103 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2793. It has itself been updated by RFC 9071.

sections.title: Why Text Needs an RTP Payload
sections.content:
This RFC defines a payload type for carrying text conversation session contents, as specified in ITU-T Recommendation T.140, inside RTP packets. Text conversation is used alone or together with video and voice in multimedia conversation services. Text is sent character by character as soon as it is available, or after a small buffering delay. Typing is slow, usually a few characters per second or less, so a packet normally carries only one or a few new characters.

T.140 requires UTF-8 text and a transport that delivers characters without duplication and in the original order. The RFC says users expect little or no lost text. The mechanism here therefore gives correct order, no duplicates, and detection and indication of loss. It also adds optional repetition of data. Because packet overhead is much larger than the text, the extra bandwidth from redundancy is minimal.

The format is named text/t140 after its MIME registration. It obsoletes RFC 2793: the text clarifies ambiguities, improves the implementation requirements learned from experience and adds explicit usage examples. The format remains compatible with RFC 2793.
sections.eli5: People who type to each other live want every letter to show up, in order. This RFC says how to put those letters into internet packets so they do.

sections.title: The text/t140 Payload and RTP Header
sections.content:
The text/t140 format is meant for text on a separate RTP session dedicated to text and not shared with other media. The payload is exactly one T140block with no additional headers specific to this payload format. A T140block holds one or more T.140 code elements, UTF-8 encoded, and it MUST contain a whole number of UTF-8 characters. A composite character sequence SHOULD be placed within one block.

The RTP header fields get these rules:

  • Payload type: assigned under the RTP profile in use; dynamic profiles identify this format by the MIME type text/t140. Redundancy needs a second payload type number.
  • Sequence number: used to detect lost and out-of-order packets.
  • Timestamp: a clock of 1000 Hz MUST be used, and sequential packets MUST NOT use the same timestamp.
  • M-bit: MUST be included. The first packet in a session and the first after an idle period SHOULD set it to one; all others MUST set it to zero.

If text must be synchronized with other media, the streams MUST be associated when the sessions are set up and MUST share a reference clock. The RFC says that association, for example through the RTCP CNAME, is outside its scope.
sections.eli5: Each packet is like an envelope holding one small note of typed letters. The envelope has a counter number so the receiver can tell if one is missing.

sections.title: Protecting Text Against Packet Loss
sections.content:
The default method, which MUST be used when no other method is selected, is redundancy as defined in RFC 2198. The original text and two redundant generations SHOULD be sent unless the application or end-to-end conditions call for other levels. Forward error correction as in RFC 2733 MAY be used instead of or together with redundancy, and text MAY be sent unprotected if network conditions allow the quality requirements of ITU-T F.703 to be met.

With redundancy, the RTP header is followed by one header per redundant block, then the redundant blocks taken from earlier packets, and finally the new primary block. Redundant data whose timestamp offset would be higher than 16383 MUST NOT be included.

RFC 2198 headers carry no sequence numbers, so three rules let a receiver work them out by counting backwards from the packet's own sequence number: each redundant block MUST repeat data already sent as primary data, redundant blocks MUST be in age order with the newest last, and all blocks from the oldest desired generation up to the one just before the primary block MUST be included. If a gap in sequence numbers appears and a later packet holds matching redundant blocks, they may be used to fill it.
sections.eli5: Every message repeats the last two messages too, like saying a phone number three times. If you miss one hearing, you still catch it on the next.

sections.title: Recommended Sender and Receiver Procedure
sections.content:
Packets are sent when there is valid T.140 data. T.140 allows buffering for at most 500 ms, and 300 ms is RECOMMENDED when nothing else is known. If no new data arrives for longer than the buffering time, the sender is in an idle period. After an idle period, new text is best sent as soon as possible, then buffered again in buffering-time intervals.

At the start of an idle period the sender SHOULD transmit an empty T140block so a receiver can quickly detect text lost just before the pause. With redundancy, packets keep going on each timer expiry, with empty primary blocks, until the last non-empty block has been sent with all intended generations of redundancy. An empty block sent as primary MUST be included as redundant data in later packets too, so that the sequence number inference still works.

Receivers find loss by gaps in the RTP sequence numbers, and MAY compare the highest sequence number with RTCP reports. Missing data SHOULD be marked with a missing text marker, as specified in ITU-T T.140 Addendum 1. A receiver that sees a packet with fewer redundancy levels than usual SHOULD treat it as if an empty block was received for each missing level. Because the format depends on sequence numbers, text/t140 is RECOMMENDED to be the only payload type in its RTP stream.

A receiver MAY hold a packet that follows a gap, if no redundant data can fill it, while waiting for the missing packet. The RFC RECOMMENDS limiting that wait to 1 second. Text that does not arrive in time is treated as lost.
sections.eli5: The sender gathers letters for a short moment, then sends them in one go. If you pause typing, it sends a little empty note so the other side knows nothing is missing.

sections.title: The cps Character Rate Parameter
sections.content:
Sometimes the rate of characters must be limited, for example when a gateway connects an IP device to a PSTN textphone and might otherwise overflow its buffer. The RFC defines the MIME parameter cps, carried in SDP as a=fmtp:<format> cps=<integer>. The integer is the maximum number of characters that may be received per second, as a mean over any 10-second interval. The default is 30.

A device that receives the parameter MUST send at or below that rate. Because cps did not exist in RFC 2793, some older implementations may not obey it, so receivers MUST be able to cope with a temporarily higher rate. For offer/answer use, cps is declarative: each side may give its own value, independent of the other.
sections.eli5: The receiver can say "please do not type faster than this". Even so, the receiver must be ready in case the sender is a little faster.

sections.title: Packet and SDP Examples
sections.content:
The RFC draws a plain text/t140 packet: the usual RTP header fields (V=2, CC=0, M bit, payload type, sequence number, a 1000 Hz timestamp and the SSRC) followed by the T.140 data. It then shows a packet with one redundant block, where the payload type is the redundancy type and a block header gives the T140 payload type, the timestamp offset and the block length of the redundant block.

Further examples show a packet whose primary block is empty, sent only to push out redundant data, and a follow-on packet with two levels of redundancy in which a zero block length stands for the empty block. The SDP examples describe text on port 11000, first without redundancy and then with two levels using RFC 2198.
sections.eli5: The examples show what the envelopes look like with no repeats, one repeat and two repeats, and how a call setup message announces them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security considerations of RFC 3550 apply. Since the format carries human conversation, encryption matters. The amount of data is low, so any encryption method MAY be applied to the T.140 contents or to whole RTP packets, and SRTP (RFC 3711) is named as a suitable choice for confidentiality. SRTP can also provide integrity protection.

For source authentication, the RFC says security measures available in the multimedia control environment SHOULD be applied at registration and session setup, so that the sender's identity is reliably tied to the person or device that set up the session. Once the session exists, SRTP MAY be used to confirm that the source stays the same.
sections.eli5: Because chats can be private, you can scramble the packets so only the other person can read them.

sections.title: Congestion Considerations
sections.content:
The congestion rules of RFC 3550, RFC 2198 and the RTP profile in use apply. Automated systems MUST NOT use this format to send large amounts of text at rates well above what a human could type. In best-effort networks, an application MUST monitor packet loss and reduce its sending rate if it sends faster than TCP would achieve over the same path, though the RFC notes that text with redundancy tolerates very high loss before this is needed.

When it must slow down, the sender SHOULD NOT cut redundancy below the default. The RECOMMENDED actions, in priority order, are: raise the minimum time between transmissions from 300 ms to 500 ms, limit the character rate, raise the time between transmissions to no more than 5 seconds, and exclude participants. If that is not enough, the only remaining action is to end the session.

As guidance, the RFC gives a load figure of 3300 bits/s for the unusually high case of 20 characters per second at three octets per character, two redundant levels and 300 ms between transmissions. With the limits applied (10 characters per second, 5 s between transmissions, one octet per character) it is 300 bits/s. It adds that this payload can serve as a last resort to keep some contact when audio and video must be stopped.
sections.eli5: Typing uses very little network. If the network gets crowded, the chat slows down gently instead of stopping, because even a slow chat can be very important.

items.title: Repeat earlier data
items.text: Each redundant block MUST hold the same data already sent as primary data.

items.title: Age order
items.text: Oldest first, with the most recent redundant block last.

items.title: No gaps
items.text: Every block from the oldest desired generation up to the one before the primary block MUST be included.
